summary: Describes a framework for using forward error correction (FEC) codes to make bulk data transfer over IP multicast more reliable. It defines what extra information must travel with the encoded data, and how new FEC codes are specified and registered with IANA. It also sets requirements for protocols that want to use these codes.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5052 sets shared rules for combining forward error correction schemes with content delivery protocols. It explains what information accompanies an encoded object and what each kind of specification must define.

subtitle: A reusable framework for carrying forward-error-correction information in content delivery protocols.

tldr.problem: Content delivery protocols need a way to use different forward error correction schemes without defining a special pairing for every protocol and code.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC separates scheme-level object information from per-packet payload identifiers and sets requirements for both FEC schemes and content delivery protocols.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3452 and defines shared encoding identifiers and a block partitioning algorithm. Congestion control must come from another building block.

today: RFC 5052 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes the Experimental RFC 3452. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 5052.

sections.title: A Shared Framework for FEC
sections.content:
Forward Error Correction (FEC) adds information that can help a receiver rebuild data when some transmitted symbols are missing. RFC 5052 defines a building block that lets content delivery protocols and FEC schemes work together without depending on each other's internal design.

The framework applies to bulk content delivery, including multicast and unicast. It defines information requirements, not the packet formats of a particular delivery protocol or the details of a specific FEC code.
sections.plainLanguage: FEC adds information that can help rebuild missing data. This RFC sets shared rules so different delivery protocols and FEC schemes can work together.

sections.title: Why FEC Helps Content Delivery
sections.content:
An encoding symbol can help receivers that lost different packets, which can reduce requests for retransmission. This is useful when one sender delivers the same object to many receivers, and the RFC also allows unicast use.

The framework covers the symbols themselves, information about symbols or source blocks, and information about the whole object. It does not define how a receiver asks a sender for particular symbols.
sections.plainLanguage: Receivers can use extra symbols to recover different missing parts of the same object. That can reduce the need for a sender to answer each receiver with a separate retransmission.

sections.title: FEC Schemes and Their Identifiers
sections.content:
An FEC scheme defines the code together with the information and procedures needed to use it. A Fully-Specified scheme has enough published detail for independent implementations; an Under-Specified scheme lacks a public complete algorithm or specification.

IANA assigns an FEC Encoding ID so a receiver can select a decoder. Values from 0 through 127 are for Fully-Specified schemes; 128 through 255 are for Under-Specified schemes. An Under-Specified scheme also uses an FEC Instance ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The scheme tells a receiver how to use a particular FEC code. Its identifier lets the receiver select the matching decoding method.

sections.title: Information for the Whole Object
sections.content:
FEC Object Transmission Information (OTI) carries information needed to decode an object. Its elements may be Mandatory, Common, or Scheme-specific. The FEC Encoding ID is the Mandatory element defined here.

Common elements can describe the object length, symbol length, source-block limits, or number of encoding symbols. The delivery protocol must transport the OTI reliably; the FEC scheme defines the meaning and encoding of the elements it uses.
sections.plainLanguage: OTI is information about the whole object, such as which FEC scheme is used and how the object is divided. The delivery protocol must get this information to receivers reliably.

sections.title: Information for Each Packet
sections.content:
The FEC Payload ID tells a decoder how the symbols in one packet relate to the object. It can identify source symbols or explain how repair symbols were constructed, and may identify their source block.

A packet carrying encoding symbols MUST include an FEC Payload ID. The FEC scheme defines its format, and the content delivery protocol defines where it appears in a data packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The payload identifier tells the receiver which object symbols a packet carries. A packet carrying encoded symbols must provide this identifier.

sections.title: What New Specifications Must Define
sections.content:
A new FEC scheme specification must define its identifier, payload identifier format, OTI meaning, and encodings. A Fully-Specified scheme must also define the code precisely enough that implementations produce the same encoding symbols and describe practical encoder and decoder algorithms.

A content delivery protocol must reliably carry required OTI and associate each data packet with its FEC Payload ID. It must define how those values are encoded and delivered.
sections.plainLanguage: A scheme specification explains how its code and identifiers work. A delivery protocol specification explains how it carries that information and each packet's identifier.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
A corrupted packet can cause a decoder to produce an unusable object, and a multicast injection may reach many receivers. The RFC recommends authenticating sources and checking the decoded object's integrity before delivery.

This building block provides no congestion control. A complete multicast content delivery protocol must provide congestion control through another building block.
sections.plainLanguage: Receivers should check who sent the data and whether the rebuilt object is intact. A complete delivery protocol must also provide congestion control separately.
